meta.name: Norwich Terrier
meta.excerpt: The Norwich Terrier is one of the smallest AKC terriers — bold, cheerful, and identified by its upright prick ears. A resilient working terrier with a happy-go-lucky personality and minimal shedding.
meta.meta_description: Norwich Terrier breed guide: prick ears, temperament, grooming, health, and care for this small but hardy and cheerful terrier breed.

intro.label: Overview
intro.heading: The Norwich Terrier: Prick-Eared, Plucky, and Full of Life
intro.html:
The Norwich Terrier is the upright-eared counterpart of the Norfolk Terrier — both breeds share the same origins, the same wiry coat, and the same spirited working terrier character. The prick ears are the defining feature: small, erect, and pointed, giving the Norwich an expression of perpetual attentiveness. This feature, combined with a slightly rounder, more open face than the Norfolk, gives the Norwich a characteristic look often described as bright-eyed and cheerful.

Like the Norfolk, the Norwich was bred in East Anglia, England, to bolt foxes from their dens and control vermin. The two varieties were the same breed until formally separated by the Kennel Club in 1964 and the AKC in 1979. Today, while the breeds are extremely similar, many fanciers feel the Norwich has a slightly bolder, more forward personality — though this is highly individual.

At 12 pounds and 10 inches, the Norwich is among the smallest working terriers. But its frame holds a remarkable amount of substance — dense bone, strong hindquarters, and a courage that makes it indifferent to its own size. Norwich Terriers have been known to stand their ground against much larger dogs and will pursue game or vermin with complete disregard for obstacles in the way.

For owners, the Norwich Terrier offers a wonderful combination of traits: low-shedding coat, long lifespan (12–15 years), sturdy good health, genuine trainability for a terrier, and a personality that tends toward the cheerful and sociable end of the terrier spectrum. It is an adaptable breed that can thrive in apartments or houses, with singles or families, as long as it receives sufficient daily exercise and mental engagement.

appearance.label: Appearance
appearance.heading: Small, Strong, and Distinctly Prick-Eared
appearance.html:
The Norwich Terrier is a compact, low, sturdy dog. The body is short and level, with good substance for its size — heavy bone and strong musculature belie the small frame. The head is slightly rounded, the muzzle wedge-shaped and strong. The prick ears are small, erect, and set wide apart on a broad skull, giving the breed its characteristic open, alert expression.

The coat is wiry, hard, and straight, lying close to the body with a distinct undercoat. It comes in red, wheaten, black and tan, or grizzle. The tail is docked to medium length in countries where legal. The overall impression is of a sturdy, determined little dog that looks ready to go to work at any moment.

temperament.label: Temperament
temperament.heading: Hardy, Cheerful, and Boldly Curious
temperament.html:
The Norwich Terrier is a genuinely happy breed. It approaches life with enthusiasm, whether exploring the garden, playing with children, or investigating a strange sound at the fence. It is affectionate with its family without being clingy, and it balances terrier independence with a willingness to engage and please.

Like all terriers, the Norwich has a prey drive and will chase small animals. It is generally good with other dogs, especially those it has been raised with, and tends to be sociable rather than aggressive in multi-dog situations. With children, it is playful and resilient — patient enough for active households, though its small size warrants supervision with very young children.

The Norwich requires daily interaction and exercise. Boredom leads to barking, digging, and inventive mischief. But a Norwich that is well-exercised and engaged is one of the most delightful small dogs you'll encounter — endlessly entertaining, surprisingly trainable, and genuinely affectionate.

mikes_take.label: Mike's Take
mikes_take.heading: Mike's Take: Bold, Happy, and Endlessly Game
mikes_take.html: The Norwich Terrier might be my favorite of the small terriers for people who want the full terrier experience without the intensity of some of the bigger, more aggressive breeds. The prick ears and that bright expression give it a permanently cheerful look that actually matches the personality. Low shedding, long-lived, adaptable — it checks most of the boxes. If you haven't considered the Norwich, you should.

care.label: Care
care.heading: Exercise and Coat Care for the Norwich Terrier
care.html:
The Norwich Terrier needs at least 30–45 minutes of active exercise daily — a combination of leash walks and off-leash play in a safely fenced area. It is an adaptable breed that can live happily in an apartment if its exercise needs are consistently met.

The wiry coat is low-maintenance compared to many breeds but does require weekly brushing with a slicker brush and metal comb. For show dogs, hand-stripping is the preferred grooming method to maintain coat texture and color. For pet dogs, professional clipping every 8–12 weeks keeps the coat tidy. Dental care, ear checks, and nail trimming complete the routine maintenance schedule.

health.label: Health
health.heading: Robust Health and Long Lifespan
health.html:
The Norwich Terrier is a hardy breed with a lifespan of 12–15 years. Upper airway syndrome (UAS) — a combination of anatomical features including an elongated soft palate and narrowed nostrils — has been identified in the breed and is a focus of health monitoring by the Norwich and Norfolk Terrier Club. Mitral valve disease can occur in older individuals. Patellar luxation and epilepsy have also been reported.

Reputable breeders screen for UAS and cardiac conditions. The Norwich Terrier Health Foundation funds ongoing health research for the breed. Ask breeders about health testing protocols before purchasing a puppy.

cost.label: Cost
cost.heading: Norwich Terrier Cost Overview
cost.html: Norwich Terrier puppies from responsible breeders typically range from $1,500 to $2,800. The breed is relatively rare and litters are small, contributing to the price. Annual costs include food ($30–$50/month), grooming ($200–$480/year for professional trimming), and routine veterinary care ($400–$700/year). Pet insurance averages $30–$55/month.

right_for_you.label: Right for You?
right_for_you.heading: Is the Norwich Terrier Right for You?
good_fit: The Norwich Terrier suits active individuals, couples, and families with older children who want a small, spirited, low-shedding companion with genuine personality
It adapts to a variety of living situations with appropriate daily exercise
Its sociable nature makes it one of the more versatile small terriers
not_fit: You work full-time with 8+ hours away from home — Norwich Terriers need 90+ min of vigorous daily activity, and under-exercised dogs of this breed often develop destructive chewing, barking, or separation anxiety

You expect a calm, quiet first 8-12 weeks — Norwich Terrier puppies, like all breeds, go through a 'puppy blues' phase of sleep loss, biting, accidents, and overwhelm that 73% of new sole-caretakers report struggling with
Homes with small pets that trigger its prey drive
But for the right owner, the Norwich Terrier is an absolutely outstanding small dog — tough, funny, loyal, and full of life

finding.label: Finding a Norwich Terrier
finding.heading: Finding a Responsible Norwich Terrier Breeder
finding.html: The Norwich and Norfolk Terrier Club (NNTC) maintains a breeder referral list through the AKC. Responsible breeders health-screen for upper airway syndrome, cardiac conditions, and patellar luxation. Wait lists are common. Terrier rescue organizations occasionally have Norwich Terriers and Norwich/Norfolk mixes available.

faq.q: How do I tell a Norwich Terrier from a Norfolk Terrier?
faq.a: Look at the ears. Norwich Terriers have erect prick ears (pointed, standing up). Norfolk Terriers have drop ears (folded forward, V-shaped). Everything else about the two breeds is nearly identical.

faq.q: Are Norwich Terriers good apartment dogs?
faq.a: Yes, with sufficient daily exercise. The Norwich adapts well to smaller living spaces as long as it gets at least 30–45 minutes of vigorous activity daily. Its vocal nature means training to manage barking is important in close-quarters living.

faq.q: Do Norwich Terriers shed a lot?
faq.a: No. The wiry coat sheds minimally — dead hair tends to stay in the coat rather than falling out, which is why regular brushing or professional stripping is needed to remove it. This makes the Norwich a good choice for people who don't want heavy shedding.
